title: Step by Step
sub: Grades 5–8 · Social Studies · How the Holocaust unfolded, 1933–1945

hero.credit: Danielle Jansen, *International Monument Auschwitz II-Birkenau 08*. CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

objective: Students will trace the Holocaust from January 1933 to May 1945 on the exhibition’s *Timeline of the Holocaust*, define it precisely — the systematic, state-sponsored persecution and murder of six million Jews by the Nazi regime and its allies and collaborators — and describe how it grew in stages: **laws** that shut Jews out, **violence** and war, **ghettos** and mass shootings, and **killing centers**. They will read the timeline’s photographs as primary sources, and weigh the choices people made.

objectives.heading: By the end of this lesson you will be able to:
objectives.why: The Holocaust did not begin with camps. Seeing each step, and the choices people made at each one, helps us recognize hatred and exclusion early, and remember that people could act differently.

materials: The *Timeline of the Holocaust* on page 3, projected or printed; the exhibition’s timeline room on a screen if you have one
connection: **Visit the exhibition:** in *The Timeline of the Holocaust*, tap any date for what happened, where, and what to look closer at; try *Put them in order*. *The Walk* opens with a film of the same history, step by step.

steps.title: Who is shut out?
script: Show three photographs from the timeline without their dates: a sign on a shop window, a printed page of laws, the signs on a perfume shop door. *“What do you see? Who is being shut out, and how?”* Then translate: the shop sign reads *Germans! Defend yourselves! Do not buy from Jews!*; the laws said Jews could not be citizens; the Vienna shop refuses Jewish customers. *“All three come from before the war. The Holocaust did not begin with camps.”*

steps.purpose: Look before any explanation: notice exclusion in ordinary places.
students: What do you see in each one?
Who is being shut out, and how?

steps.title: Step by step
script: Read the exhibition’s definition: the Holocaust, also known as the *Shoah* (Hebrew for “catastrophe”), was the systematic persecution and murder of six million Jewish men, women, and children. Then the people before the number: Jews had lived in Europe for more than two thousand years; in 1933 about nine million lived there. In Leipzig in April 1929, Berta Rosenheim held a large paper school cone on her first day of school.

screen.text: It did not happen all at once. It happened step by step.
screen.cite: The Walk · the film’s opening words

steps.purpose: Define the Holocaust precisely, and see the people before the number.
students: What does *step by step* tell you about how it happened?

steps.title: Four steps
script: Walk through the four steps (page 3). **Shut out by law:** Dachau, for people who opposed the Nazis, in March 1933; the boycott; the burned books; the Nuremberg Laws. **Violence and war:** Kristallnacht, when more than 1,400 synagogues were burned; the war from September 1939; the secret murder of disabled people. **Walled in and shot:** more than 400,000 Jews shut in the Warsaw ghetto; from June 1941, mass shootings — 33,771 Jews at Babi Yar in two days. **Killing centers:** at Wannsee in January 1942, fifteen officials met to plan the “Final Solution”; trains carried Jews from across Europe, which the Nazis called “resettlement to the east.” Explain both terms as words that hid murder.

steps.purpose: Set out the four stages the timeline shows, and how each made the next possible.
students: Name one event from each step.
How did each step make the next one possible?

steps.title: A child’s words
script: Read Steven Frank’s words. *“The first steps were laws and signs. What did they mean to a five-year-old?”*

screen.text: “I was suddenly different from all my other friends. I was no longer allowed to play in the park, my father could not take public transport to work; I couldn’t go into the swimming pool or the zoo.”
screen.cite: Steven Frank, five when the Nazis occupied the Netherlands

steps.purpose: Hear what the first steps meant to one child.
students: Which change would a neighbor have noticed?

steps.title: Choose a handout
script: Students choose a handout. All three levels work from the same timeline and the same years.

levels.name: Green Level
levels.summary: Read about Jewish life before 1933; sort ten events into the four steps; read Steven Frank’s words closely; finish *First… Then… Later…* to show how one step led to the next.

levels.name: Yellow Level
levels.summary: Read two timeline photographs as primary sources, then chart what six events took away and how each prepared the next. Explain, with three events, why the Holocaust did not begin with camps.

levels.name: Red Level
levels.summary: Compare three descriptions of the Wannsee Conference, question a photograph staged as propaganda, then argue whether the Holocaust was inevitable, using the choices people made.

steps.purpose: Practice reading the timeline and its sources at the right level of challenge.
students: Choose Green, Yellow or Red. All three levels work from the same timeline.

steps.title: The timeline
script: Project the timeline. Ask each group to point to the first entry they would call persecution, and to one place where people made a choice. Let a Red Level reader give the *Genocide never just happens* quotation and say what circumstances the timeline shows being created.

screen.caption: The Timeline of the Holocaust: twenty dates, in the exhibition’s words

cells: Adolf Hitler is appointed Chancellor of Germany
Dachau, the first concentration camp, is established
Nationwide boycott of Jewish businesses in Germany
The Nuremberg Laws are enacted, stripping Jews of citizenship and banning marriage between Jews and non-Jews
Germany annexes Austria (Anschluss); persecution of Austrian Jews begins
*Kristallnacht* (Night of Broken Glass): Synagogues are burned, Jewish businesses are destroyed, and thousands of Jews are arrested
Germany invades Poland, starting World War II
Nazis begin *Aktion T4*, the euthanasia program targeting disabled individuals
The Warsaw Ghetto is established, confining hundreds of thousands of Jews
Germany invades the Soviet Union; Einsatzgruppen begin mass shootings of Jews in occupied territories
Over 33,000 Jews are murdered during the Babi Yar massacre near Kyiv
Chelmno, the first extermination camp, begins operations
The Wannsee Conference formalizes the “Final Solution,” planning the extermination of Jews
Mass extermination begins at Belzec, followed by Sobibor and Treblinka that spring and summer
The Warsaw Ghetto Uprising, where Jews resist deportation to extermination camps, occurs
D-Day: Allied forces invade Normandy, opening a Western front
Soviet forces liberate Majdanek, the first major concentration camp to be freed
Germany surrenders, ending World War II in Europe and the Holocaust

steps.purpose: Pull the lesson together on the timeline, and ask where it could have been stopped.
students: Point to the first step you would call *persecution*.
Where might people have acted differently?

steps.title: Look back
script: Put the objectives back on the screen, asked as questions: *“Can you now…?”* For each one, students show a thumb up, sideways or down. Ask one student to answer each aloud; for the last, ask a Red Level reader.
